content: The treatment criteria for the study required participants to have undergone treatment for at least four weeks, reside in the LPEP pilot area, and have one or more household members or neighbors as contacts. Participants also needed to be willing to disclose their disease status to their identified contacts. A systematic literature search was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of vaccines for leprosy prevention, both with and without chemoprophylaxis, among contacts of leprosy patients and the general population. The search included studies published between 2010 and January 2017, using databases such as MEDLINE and Embase. The search strategy incorporated MeSH terms and keywords like leprosy, immunoprophylaxis, chemoprevention, ICRC, IDRI, and Mycobacterium. No restrictions were applied regarding study design or language. The eligibility criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, and case-control studies that assessed immunoprophylaxis and/or chemoprophylaxis for leprosy prevention. Interventions included BCG vaccination at birth, BCG revaccination, other vaccines, and single-dose rifampicin (SDR) combined with BCG. Comparators were no vaccination or no revaccination. Participants included both adults and children who were contacts of multibacillary (MB) and paucibacillary (PB) leprosy patients, as well as the general population with a BCG scar. The primary outcomes were the occurrence of leprosy and adverse effects, while secondary outcomes included feasibility, acceptability, and costs. The systematic search identified 87 citations, of which 19 full-text articles were reviewed. The quality of the included RCTs ranged from low to moderate. Evidence suggested that BCG vaccination at birth is effective in preventing leprosy compared to placebo or no BCG, with a protective effect of 57% (95% CI: 24–75%) at two years. Combining SDR with BCG showed an even higher protective effect of 80% (95% CI: 50–92%), indicating that SDR may enhance the effectiveness of childhood BCG vaccination. Studies on BCG combined with killed Mycobacterium leprae or Mycobacterium w vaccines also demonstrated significant protective effects. For example, the ICRC vaccine reduced leprosy incidence by 66% (95% CI: 48–77%) compared to placebo. Similarly, Mycobacterium w vaccination showed a protective effect of up to 69% after nine years when both patients and their contacts were vaccinated. However, most studies focused on BCG and its variants, with limited data on other vaccines. Adverse event data were also scarce. The evidence was synthesized using the WHO/GRADE approach, considering factors like risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. The overall quality of evidence varied, with some studies showing moderate quality and others low quality. In conclusion, BCG vaccination, particularly when combined with SDR or other immunoprophylactic strategies, appears to be effective in reducing leprosy incidence among contacts of leprosy patients and the general population. Further research is needed to explore the effectiveness of other vaccines and to address gaps in data on adverse events and long-term outcomes.
